lessons.title: Introduction, Finite Automata, and Regular Expressions

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.404J Lecture 1: Introduction, Finite Automata, Regular Expressions (F2020)

notes.summary: Sipser's Theory of Computation, taught in the Fall 2020 recorded edition: what can be computed, and at what cost? Lecture 1 introduces deterministic finite automata as language recognizers and regular expressions as language descriptions — two faces of the same class of languages, a correspondence you'll soon prove.
notes.focus: For one small DFA, write the regular expression it accepts by inspecting state structure. Building the correspondence early makes the proofs feel inevitable.

notes.summary: Nondeterminism — guessing as a computational resource — and the subset construction converting any NFA to an equivalent DFA (possibly exponentially larger). Closure properties (union, concatenation, star) fall out constructively. This is the machinery your Nand2Tetris tokenizer and every regex engine quietly relies on.
notes.focus: Run the subset construction on a small NFA and count the reachable states. Exponential blowup on paper explains why regex engines go catastrophic.

lessons.title: The Pumping Lemma and Non-Regular Languages

notes.summary: The first impossibility result: finite memory cannot count, so {0^n 1^n} is not regular. The pumping lemma formalizes the pigeonhole argument — long strings must revisit a state, and that loop can be pumped. Learning to wield the lemma (as a game against an adversary) is the course's introduction to proving things IMPOSSIBLE.
notes.focus: Prove {ww} non-regular with the pumping lemma, writing the adversary's move at each step. The game framing keeps quantifier order straight.

notes.summary: Adding a stack unlocks structure: context-free grammars generate nested languages (balanced parens, arithmetic), and PDAs recognize them. The CFG-to-PDA construction is constructive. This is the exact theory behind parsing — your N2T project-10 recursive descent parser is a CFG walkthrough, and CS143's parser generators are this lecture industrialized.
notes.focus: Trace a derivation of a balanced-parentheses string in a small CFG, drawing the parse tree. Then note which derivation order your own N2T parser used.

notes.summary: The Church-Turing thesis: TMs capture effective computation — everything from laptops to lambda calculus computes the same class. TM variants (multi-tape, nondeterministic) add convenience but not power. Every language you know, every computer you'll use: a TM in fancy clothing. This is the floor of computation.
notes.focus: Design a TM for {0^n 1^n} (the language PDAs couldn't do without a stack). The machine is short — and it establishes what 'more powerful' means.

notes.summary: Decision problems for the lower levels are decidable: emptiness, equivalence of DFAs, CFG membership (CYK). But the halting problem — does this TM halt on this input? — is undecidable, by diagonalization. The proof technique (self-reference) is the same trick behind Cantor, Russell, and Godel, and it lands here as the first law of computational limits.
notes.focus: Reproduce the halting-problem diagonalization from memory. It is six lines — and knowing them cold is knowing the boundary of computing.

notes.summary: Undecidability spreads by reduction: if solving B would solve the halting problem, B is undecidable too. Rice's theorem (any nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable) is the industrial-strength version. Recognizable vs decidable languages (semi-decision vs decision) refines the map of what's even approachable.
notes.focus: Reduce ATM to EQTM in writing. When the reduction pattern (assume solver, build halting oracle) is automatic, the whole unit is yours.

notes.summary: Cost enters the theory: P as feasible, NP as verifiable, and the question of the century. Time hierarchy theorems prove that more time really computes more languages. This lecture is the rigorous version of the cliff edge you met in 6.046J — now you can define the terms precisely.
notes.focus: Write the formal definitions of P and NP for yourself, then verify SAT is in NP. Precision here is what separates understanding from vibes.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.404J Lecture 14: P and NP, SAT (F2020)

notes.summary: Cook-Levin: SAT is NP-complete — every NP problem reduces to it. The 3SAT-to-clique-to-vertex-cover chain then propagates completeness through the classics. Combined with 6.046J's algorithmic side, you now hold both halves: how to prove hardness AND how to cope (approximation, heuristics).
notes.focus: Redraw the reduction diagram (3SAT -> CLIQUE -> VC -> IS) from memory with the gadget for each edge. The diagram IS the unit.

notes.summary: Space as the resource: Savitch's theorem (NSPACE(f) in SPACE(f^2)), PSPACE (games like generalized chess live there), and the L vs NL distinction with the NL=coNL surprise. The reachability-by-DFS-in-log-space construction is the technical heart — and the notes carry it in full.
notes.focus: Verify Savitch's recursion on a tiny graph reachability instance by hand. The squaring in the space bound becomes concrete once you trace it.

notes.summary: The workhorse technique of advanced undecidability: encode a TM's full execution trace as a single string, then reduce problems ABOUT that trace to problems about grammars and machines. CFG-ambiguity and Post's Correspondence Problem both fall to histories. Mastering this method is what lets you prove undecidability for languages beyond the classics.
concepts: When to reach for the technique
notes.focus: Write the history of a 3-step TM computation explicitly, then reread the CFG-ambiguity reduction with it in hand. The reduction becomes mechanical once the encoding is concrete.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the automata hierarchy: regular languages, pumping, CFGs/PDAs, TMs, and undecidability. Exams in this course are proof-writing under time — statements, quantifier discipline, and adversary games. Your 6.042J proof training from term 1 is the direct prerequisite here.
notes.focus: Rewrite your three best proofs from memory, checking that every quantifier is in the right order. Sloppy quantifiers are the #1 point leak.

notes.summary: The close ties theory to its foundations: Godel's incompleteness as self-reference's deepest form, the recursion theorem, and the full hierarchy map (regular < context-free < decidable < recognizable). Your synthesis artifact: the one-page tower of computation with the proof technique that separates each level — the field, compressed.
notes.focus: Draw the tower from memory: each level, its machine, its pumping/closure/limitation, and its separation technique. That page is your certificate in the theory of computation.
